title: Mercenary vs missionary: match what you build to your core motivation
summary: Jake Castillo explains why six years of "discipline problems" in consulting were really a motivation mismatch. He splits operators into mercenaries (money-driven) and missionaries (need to care about the thing) and gives seven questions to ask before committing to a project, so you don't burn two years operating as the wrong type.

principles.text: Ask the identity question (mercenary or missionary) before the market question when choosing what to build.
principles.quote: But you should ask the identity question first, because it determines whether you'll still be putting in the necessary hours at fourteen months in.

principles.text: Mercenaries can grind boring, high-margin businesses for years; you don't need passion for the product.
principles.quote: If you're a mercenary, go find the boring high-margin thing and grind it out.

principles.text: Missionaries can't sustain effort on something they find pointless, even if the margins are great.
principles.quote: Put a missionary on a boring product with great margins and they'll quit in month four, and they won't be able to explain why, and they'll feel like a flake about it.

principles.text: Lack of focus is often a motivation mismatch, not a discipline problem.
principles.quote: The thing that six years of performance reviews couldn't fix, that no amount of discipline touched, evaporated the moment the work was mine and mattered to me.

principles.text: Test commitment by picturing the boring middle of the business and doing it daily for a year.
principles.quote: What's the boring middle of this business? Every business has one. Support tickets, ad reviews, contracts, reconciliation.

principles.text: Don't pick as one type and operate as the other; that's how you burn two years.
principles.quote: The point is to stop picking as one and operating as the other, because that's the version where you burn two years and call yourself lazy at the end of it.
